full_judgment: 11. It has been urged that the Magistrate acted illegally by declaring title in a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In the instant case it appears that the learned Magistrate clearly found the first opposite party entitled to possession of the land and also of the standing paddy over which a dispute was reported by the Police. A Magistrate need not decide any title to any property in a proceeding under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court is only to find out actual possession and order the same to be retained on delivery-a kind of a status quo in contradiction to any finding as to any right to possess which meant ultimate title to the property. This is for the Civil Court to decide. In order to find out actual possession on the day of the dispute Magistrate must not find possession on the basis of any alleged title or right to possess but on the basis of possession alone to the extent and manner a property is capable of being possessed. But the Magistrate in finding possession may incidentally enquire in to the rights of the parties to the property in question only to corroborate the evidence as to possession on record in favour of a party. This the court can do on the presumption of law that possession follows title. This question of title can also be gone into by the Magistrate when evidence as to possession is balanced between the parties. Hence the court had rightly found that the first opposite party not only is entitled to the disputed crop but also that it were they who had grown the paddy and I find no illegality in such a finding.
